His measurements and his elite performance in the athletic drills are the biggest reasons why. Would a team actually consider him in the first round? The Cavs, Heat and Warriors are all real possibilities.

June 6 Update: Duke's Miles Plumlee didn't wow anyone in four years at Duke, but he's generating significant buzz thanks to some great individual workouts and a strong performance in the Minnesota group workout last weekend.

I see why NBA teams are intrigued. While Plumlee didn't show particularly well at Duke, he looks terrific in the drills and 5-on-5 settings I saw in Chicago. He's strong, physical and jumps out of the gym. Duke has been a very perimeter oriented team the past few years and Plumlee rarely had plays called for him. He did his work on the boards, but little else that stood out.

Part of what is driving the interest is Plumlee's physical abilities. He measured with a 41-inch vertical in the Minnesota workouts.

I've been collecting pre-draft athletic testing numbers since 2001. The tallest player ever to hit 41 inches or higher was Jamario Moon (at 6-7 3/4). Plumlee measured 6-11 1/4 in Minnesota.

The highest a player 6-11 or taller has ever jumped in the testing is 38 1/2 inches by Steven Hunter back in 2001.

Clearly your vertical jump doesn't determine whether you'll be a great NBA player. But factor in Plumlee's size, NBA body and toughness on the boards and a number of GMs are convinced he could be an athletic rebounder and shot blocker off the bench for them in the mold of Jeff Foster.

Nov 25 Update: A handful of scouts sitting next to me argued all week about whether Plumlee would get drafted. He looks the part. He's strong, a great athlete and has good size. But he doesn't produce. Some felt he has the profile to be a good backup big man in the league. Others scoffed at the idea. I'm impressed with the idea of Plumlee -- but not with the execution. If I were a GM, I'd probably pass.

Apr 12 Update: Miles doesn't get nearly the same amount of love that his brother Mason does. He's not as good of an athlete and has already been surpassed by his brother statistically and in playing time. But he's big, physical and rebounds and may have a shot as a second round pick his senior year.

This is a bit of a reach by the Pacers. Plumlee averaged 6.6 ppg and 7.1 rpg as a senior at Duke -- underwhelming numbers, to say the least. He tested with a great vertical leap and he's strong as a bull. He reminds the Pacers of a young Jeff Foster. -- Chad Ford

Hummel returned to have a very good senior season, averaging 16.4 ppg and shooting 38 percent from 3 despite the fact that he still wasn't 100 percent recovered from his last surgery.

June 25 Update: There has been talk about Jones getting a promise in the late first round. If he's received it, we can't find it. Some teams are high on him, but it wouldn't be shocking if he ended up somewhere in the later part of the second round either.

Dec 26 Update: While Perry Jones struggled in his matchup against West Virginia, another Jones continued his torrid pace this season. WVU's Kevin Jones has been dominant on both ends of the court all year, averaging 21 ppg, 12 rpg and a whopping 32.35 PER. Against Baylor, he scored 28 points and grabbed 17 boards, but it wasn't an isolated game. He had 30 and 12 versus Kansas State and 29 and 13 versus Alcorn State this season. Not bad for a player who declared for the draft last season and heard nothing but crickets from NBA teams.

For the first three years of his college career, Jones has been a borderline NBA prospect known for his motor, offensive rebounding and ability to stretch the defense with his jumper.

Jones' lack of size combined with a game that is decidedly below the rim have kept him on the margins for the past two seasons. But with his increased willingness to go inside and prove that he can score and rebound over bigger and more athletic defenders (Baylor's front line is as long and as athletic as they come), Jones may yet find his way onto an NBA roster.

Apr 21 Update: Jones is a long forward who plays hard all the time and can shoot the basketball with range. He's coming off a rocky junior season that saw his shooting percentages plummet. But the league is always interested in bigs that can shoot it. A potential second round pick.

Mar 11 Update: Jones has had a bit of a disappointing season. Scouts came in with high expectations for him, but his games appears to have stagnated somewhat this year. In fact, in some ways it's regressed. Jones shooting percentages plummeted this year and he disappeared in games. He's flirting with declaring for the 2011 NBA Draft, but if he does, it looks like he's a second-round pick at best. He may need one more year at West Virginia.

Jan 12 2009 Update: While Devin Ebanks is the Mountaineers' best draft prospect on paper, on the court, more and more NBA scouts are pointing toward a different sophomore, Kevin Jones. Jones doesn't have quite the versatility that Ebanks possesses, but he has consistently been the better player on the court over the course of the season. Scouts like a number of things about Jones. He is a workhorse on both ends of the ball. He's got a terrific motor. Like Ebanks, Jones has an impressive physical profile, highlighted by a 7-foot-4 inch wingspan, which allows him to play bigger than he is. He also has filled out to the point that he can be an effective scoring presence in the paint. Unlike Ebanks, who hasn't been able to buy a jumper this season, Jones is shooting a red-hot 62 percent from the field and 45 percent from 3. But Jones is equally comfortable posting up and scoring in the paint. Finally, Jones has proven to be a terrific offensive rebounder, averaging an impressive four offensive boards per game. While I'm still waiting on a consensus from NBA teams, enough franchises now have him ranked somewhere in the mid- to late-first round that he's getting close to cracking our top 30.

June 14 Update: Papanikolaou was one of the stars of Olympiacos' upset championship win at the Euroleague Final Four in Istanbul in May. While not a great shooter, he did not miss a shot in two games on a pressure-packed stage that rivaled any NBA playoff game or NCAA tournament game.

While he did not compete at the camp, the 6-8 Papanikolaou interviewed with a number of teams and was measured for vitals before flying back to Greece to train with the Greek national team.

He's skinny and still looks like a teenager, but when he's on the floor, he makes things happen. He has a way of getting his hands on just about everything.

Satoransky is playing in Spain this season for Seville and isn't getting real minutes for his club. But a number of NBA GMs and scouts I spoke with still think very highly of him. "If he were to declare," one international NBA scout told me, "I'm not sure how you could justify passing on him after the lottery. The kid is just a terrific player. He knows how to play."

Right now we have Satoransky ranked in the second round, but as we get closer to the draft, international players tend to rise. I definitely could see a team taking a flier on him late in the first round and then stashing him over in Europe for development for a few more years.

Jun 8 Update: If you were to poll NBA GMs and ask them which prospect has the brightest future in the NBA, I think they would unanimously pick Satoransky, a skinny point forward who finds a way to get his hands on virtually every ball. He is active on the boards and is a great passer. Plus, the 18-year-old is willing to mix it up with anyone, despite being the youngest player on the floor.

He has to get stronger and improve his jump shot, but he has a big-time feel for the game and is pretty explosive athletically. He's moving from the Czech Republic to Spain this year to play in Seville. If he can put up strong numbers there, he could be the "it" guy from Europe next year.

Satoransky will stay in Europe for at least a couple of years, probably. He's a scrappy player who plays like a point forward. If he could shoot he could have gone much higher. Has a nose for the ball. -- Chad Ford

June 14 Update: Shengelia played well enough at the Eurocamp that he is staying in the draft, with a strong likelihood that a team has already "promised" to take him in the second round later this month. He's always been a prolific scorer at the junior level in Europe and did nothing this week to harm that reputation.

Armed with a sneaky quick first step, a rugged frame at 6-9½ and 228 pounds and an ability finish from all angles around the basket, Shengelia is a power forward who could develop into a second-unit scorer for an NBA team in time. He's held back at the moment by an inconsistent jump shot. He's going to have to defend his position as well, and that will be an issue when he arrives in the league.

Ultimately, Shengelia is likely to be another guy whom an NBA team leaves in Europe the next couple of years. He'll turn just 21 in the fall, so I like him as a long-term gamble. There are not a lot of guys in this draft who can score like he does. -- Fran Fraschilla

June 25 Update: Acy is a crazy athlete with a terrific motor. He?s not particularly skilled, but could be a nice bench player at the next level.

Dec 28 Update: We've also discussed Acy here previously and there isn't much more to add. He's undersized and lacks a lot of skills offensively, but he's so long, explosive and relentless in the paint that you quickly forget his deficiencies. Sitting courtside and watching him live, it's hard not to come away in love with his motor. He truly tries to go after every ball and can dominate the game at both ends. If his teammate Perry Jones had that motor, he'd be far and away the clear favorite for the No. 1 pick.

Acy's small stature (he's probably 6-foot-7 at best) will limit his ceiling somewhat. But all of the scouts I spoke with in Honolulu loved him and see him as a potential mid to late first-round pick.

Nov 23 Update: Acy drew some fans among NBA scouts when they all flocked to Baylor to watch Ekpe Udoh last season. He drew in even more with his play this summer as a camp counselor.

Acy's 25-point, 11-rebound performance against LaSalle may have been his coming-out party. He also had an 18-point, 14-rebound game against Lipscomb and a 20-point, 12-rebound performance against Grambling State. He's a bit undersized to be a full-time 4 in the NBA, but his length and his explosive leaping ability make up for some of his weaknesses.

Aug 9 Update: Last season Ekpe Udoh got all the love, and now Perry Jones is stealing the spotlight. But more and more scouts are starting to see the light when it comes to Acy. The crazy-long, athletic forward doesn't really have a position or even a discernible NBA skill set yet. But his energy, elite leaping ability, speed and nose for the ball all had scouts praising him at the adidas Nations camp. If he can add some sort of detectable offensive game and a little strength, he'll have a legit shot at the first round.

Acy is a high-energy, rebounding forward. He's very aggressive and he tries to dunk everything. He's a little undersized for his position and he lacks face-the-basket skills. But he'll add toughness to Toronto. -- Chad Ford

June 25 Update: Odom is undersized for his position, but he's strong and athletic and can really shoot the basketball. The Clippers, who hold the No. 53 pick, need all the help they can get at the 2, and Johnson-Odom can come in and play right away.

July 11, 2011 Update: I don't know if Johnson-Odom will be a first-round selection or even get drafted, but he will play in the NBA because he is a junk yard dog and a superb athlete. He was among a number of solid Big East guards who impressed at the LeBron James Nike Skills Academy camp, like UConn's Shabazz Napier, Syracuse's Scoop Jardine and Maalik Wayns of Villanova. They will battle each other all season.

First of all, Johnson-Odom's mental approach, I believe, comes from being an obscure national recruit after one season in junior college and it carries over to how he approaches the game. His mentality of toughness along with his combination of strength and quickness makes him an outstanding defender. It is something he can hang his hat on this coming season with NBA scouts and, more importantly, his coach, Buzz Williams.

He carries over the aggressiveness on the defensive end with an attacking style on offense. Although Johnson-Odom is a left-handed jump shooter, he is ambidextrous around the rim and he does get to the rim with force, especially in the open court. And, while he didn't shoot from the outside as well as I have seen him, he is a career 41 percent 3-point shooter at Marquette.

Johnson-Odom should be a huge catalyst for Williams' team this season as one of the Big East's best guards. Based on what I saw this past week, he will be on an NBA scout's "must see" list as a result. -- By Fran Fraschilla

Johnson-Odom is a tough, physical guard who, if he was three or four inches taller, would've gone much higher in the draft. He can shoot the ball and plays great defense. I can see why he would fit in L.A. -- Chad Ford

Jan 17 Update: Scouts are really warming up to Campbell senior Eric Griffin. A long and athletic forward with explosive leaping ability and a string of highlight reel dunks, Griffin currently ranks in the top 30 of John Hollinger's college PER. That's pretty amazing when you consider that Griffin hasn't been playing the game that long and is really just coming into his own. While he's still a ways away from a lock to be drafted, a number of teams think he could sneak into the end of the first round.

Dec 4 Update: A viral video on YouTube of Griffin dunking everything against NC A&T is making the rounds and when you see his combination of length and athleticism -- he's intriguing. He's also been very efficient in the early going. He's relatively new to the game, so it looks like he's still a ways away from his ceiling. He's definitely someone to keep an eye on.
